sourceEvidence.claim: H influenzae entry part 1 (coccobacillary rod, respiratory droplets; nontypeable strains dominate post-vaccine; IgA protease; chocolate agar factors V [NAD+] and X [hematin]; S aureus satellitism — lines 83-93)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Small gram ⊝ (coccobacillary) rod. Transmitted
through respiratory droplets. Nontypeable
(unencapsulated) strains are the most common
cause of mucosal infections (otitis media,
conjunctivitis, bronchitis) as well as invasive
infections since the vaccine for capsular type b
was introduced. Produces IgA protease.
Culture on chocolate agar, which contains
factors V (NAD+) and X (hematin) for growth;
can also be grown with S aureus, which
provides factor V via RBC hemolysis.

sourceEvidence.claim: H influenzae entry part 3 (the type b vaccine: polyribosylribitol phosphate conjugated to diphtheria toxoid, 2-18 months; does not cause the flu; treatment and prophylaxis — lines 99-106)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Vaccine contains type b capsular polysaccharide
(polyribosylribitol phosphate) conjugated
to diphtheria toxoid or other protein. Given
between 2 and 18 months of age.
Does not cause the flu (influenza virus does).
Treatment: amoxicillin +/− clavulanate for
mucosal infections; ceftriaxone for meningitis;
rifampin prophylaxis for close contacts.

sourceEvidence.claim: B cepacia complex entry (aerobic, catalase ⊕; pneumonia in underlying lung disease such as cystic fibrosis; multidrug resistant; relative contraindication to lung transplant)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Aerobic, catalase ⊕, gram ⊝ rod. Causes pneumonia in patients with underlying lung disease, such
as cystic fibrosis. Often multidrug resistant. Infection is a relative contraindication to undergoing
lung transplant due to its association with poor outcomes.

sourceEvidence.claim: B pertussis entry (aerobic coccobacillus; pertussis toxin disables Gi; adenylate cyclase toxin ↑ cAMP; tracheal cytotoxin; the three ▘-bulleted stages; Tdap/DTaP; lymphocytosis; macrolides or TMP-SMX)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Bordetella pertussis

Gram ⊝, aerobic coccobacillus. Virulence factors include pertussis toxin (disables Gi), adenylate
cyclase toxin (↑ cAMP), and tracheal cytotoxin (destroys respiratory ciliated epithelium). Three
clinical stages:
▘ Catarrhal—low-grade fevers, coryza.
▘ Paroxysmal—paroxysms of intense cough followed by inspiratory “whoop” (“whooping cough”),
posttussive vomiting.
▘ Convalescent—gradual recovery of chronic cough.
Prevented by Tdap, DTaP vaccines (Tdap for preTeens and adulTs, DTaP for chilDren).
Produces lymphocytosis (unlike most acute bacterial infections).
Treatment: macrolides; if allergic use TMP-SMX.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: Brucella entry (aerobic coccobacillus; contaminated animal products, unpasteurized milk; survives in RES macrophages; noncaseating granulomas; undulant fever, night sweats, arthralgia; doxycycline + rifampin or streptomycin)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Brucella

Gram ⊝, aerobic coccobacillus. Transmitted via ingestion of contaminated animal products (eg,
unpasteurized milk). Survives in macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system. Can form noncaseating granulomas. Typically presents with undulant fever, night sweats, and arthralgia.
Treatment: doxycycline + rifampin or streptomycin.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: L pneumophila entry part 1 (poor gram stain — silver stain; charcoal yeast extract with iron and cysteine; urine antigen; hyponatremia + elevated transaminases; aerosol transmission from water; cruise ships, nursing homes; NO person-to-person transmission; macrolide or quinolone)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Legionella
pneumophila

Gram ⊝ rod. Gram stains poorly—use silver
stain. Grow on charcoal yeast extract medium
with iron and cysteine. Detected by presence of
antigen in urine. Labs may show hyponatremia
and elevated transaminases.
Aerosol transmission from environmental water
source (eg, air conditioning systems, hot
water tanks). Outbreaks associated with cruise
ships, nursing homes. No person-to-person
transmission.
Treatment: macrolide or quinolone.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: L pneumophila entry part 2 (the FA campfire mnemonic, printed — verification only; Legionnaires disease with inline photo marker A; Pontiac fever)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Think of a French legionnaire (soldier) with
his silver helmet, sitting around a campfire
(charcoal) with his iron dagger—he is missing
his sister (cysteine).
Legionnaires’ disease—severe pneumonia
(often unilateral and lobar A ), fever, GI and
CNS symptoms. Risk factors include older age,
tobacco smoking, chronic lung disease.
Pontiac fever—mild flulike symptoms.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: P aeruginosa entry part 1 (aerobic, motile, catalase ⊕; non-lactose fermenting; oxidase ⊕; water; acidic-environment virulence; grapelike odor; the printed PSEUDOMONAS association block with the 'healthcareassociated' hyphen-drop)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Aeruginosa—aerobic; motile, catalase ⊕, gram ⊝
rod. Non-lactose fermenting. Oxidase ⊕.
Frequently found in water. Increased virulence
in acidic environments. Has a grapelike odor.
PSEUDOMONAS is associated with:
Pneumonia, Sepsis, Ecthyma gangrenosum,
UTIs, Diabetes, Osteomyelitis, Mucoid
polysaccharide capsule, Otitis externa
(swimmer’s ear), Nosocomial (healthcareassociated) infections (eg, catheters,
equipment), Addiction (injection drug use),
Skin infections (eg, hot tub folliculitis, wound
infection in burn victims).
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: P aeruginosa entry part 2 (mucoid capsule → CF chronic pneumonia via biofilm; the PEEP toxin set with inline green-pigment photo marker A)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Mucoid polysaccharide capsule may contribute
to chronic pneumonia in patients with cystic
fibrosis due to biofilm formation.
Produces PEEP: Phospholipase C (degrades cell
membranes); Endotoxin (fever, shock); Exotoxin
A (inactivates EF-2); green Pigment A .

sourceEvidence.claim: P aeruginosa entry part 3 (corneal ulcers/keratitis in contact lens wearers; ecthyma gangrenosum with inline photo marker B; the ▘-bulleted treatment list with 'piperacillintazobactam' hyphen-drop; aminoglycoside monotherapy avoided)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Corneal ulcers/keratitis in contact lens wearers/
minor eye trauma.
Ecthyma gangrenosum—rapidly progressive,
necrotic cutaneous lesion B caused by
Pseudomonas bacteremia. Typically seen in
immunocompromised patients.
Treatments:
▘ Antipseudomonal penicillins in combination
with β-lactamase inhibitor (eg, piperacillintazobactam)
▘ 3rd- and 4th-generation cephalosporins (eg,
ceftazidime, cefepime)
▘ Monobactams
▘ Fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin,
levofloxacin)
▘ Carbapenems
Despite antipseudomonal activity,
aminoglycoside monotherapy is avoided due to
poor performance in acidic environments.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

kypExtensions.summary: The reservoir-to-disease reading (the exposure history as the diagnostic test: the dorm/barracks for meningococci with Waterhouse-Friderichsen as the adrenal cross-link, the cruise-ship water aerosol for Legionella with its no-person-to-person rule, the unpasteurized-milk macrophage survival of Brucella, the water-and-acid story of Pseudomonas with ecthyma and the CF biofilm); the conjugate-vaccine column (Hib PRP-toxoid) alongside the antigenic-variation non-vaccine of the gonococcus; the Exotoxin A-EF-2 link back to diphtheria; and the tree's leaves as the pre-load of the enterics and GI chapters — labeled as integrations.
kypExtensions.rationale: The source prints the tree and entries without the reservoir synthesis or the cross-chapter wiring; these integrations are KYP's design.
